human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a well-motivated empirical contribution to dialogue evaluation by reformulating the problem as supervised learning and demonstrating that learned models substantially outperform word-overlap metrics. The core claims (word-overlap metrics fail; learned models achieve higher correlation) are robustly supported by comprehensive empirical evaluation. However, the contribution has important limitations that should be acknowledged: (1) Moderate absolute correlation (r=0.436) leaves 81% unexplained variance, raising questions about practical utility for single-response evaluation; (2) System-level evaluation uses only 4 models with marginal statistical significance (p=0.046), limiting confidence in generalization to larger model sets; (3) Generalization to unseen models is inconsistent and unexplained (Dual Encoder failure r=0.027); (4) Domain specificity to Twitter is not validated; (5) Multiple acknowledged limitations (generic response bias, conservative prediction bias, appropriateness criterion narrowness) are deferred to future work. The paper makes a meaningful first step toward learned dialogue evaluation but requires methodological refinement and validation on additional domains and model types before claims can be considered definitive. Recommend acceptance with major revisions addressing: (a) confidence intervals and statistical power analysis for system-level results; (b) investigation of Dual Encoder generalization failure; (c) quantification of generic response bias and conservative prediction bias; (d) preliminary domain transfer validation; (e) ablation studies on alternative architectures and pre-training objectives. The paper's transparency about limitations is commendable and should be preserved in revision.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes a solid contribution to dialogue evaluation by demonstrating that learned models substantially outperform word-overlap metrics. The core empirical findings are well-supported. To strengthen the contribution, address the following: (1) Provide confidence intervals for all correlation estimates using bootstrap resampling; conduct statistical power analysis for system-level evaluation (n=4 is very small); discuss practical implications of r=0.436 utterance-level correlation and specify acceptable deployment thresholds. (2) Investigate why Dual Encoder fails to generalize (r=0.027): analyze architectural differences, response characteristics, and error patterns; test whether failure is model-specific or indicates fundamental limitation; provide mechanistic explanation rather than simply reporting the failure. (3) Quantify generic response bias and conservative prediction bias: measure correlation between ADEM scores and response length/genericity; analyze failure cases in Table 5; implement and evaluate proposed mitigation strategies (censoring, adversarial evaluation) rather than deferring to future work. (4) Validate domain transfer: evaluate on at least one additional dialogue domain (Reddit, customer service, or task-oriented dialogue); discuss which aspects of ADEM are domain-specific vs. domain-agnostic; quantify cost of domain-specific pre-training. (5) Provide comprehensive ablation studies: compare alternative architectures (Transformer, CNN, attention), alternative pre-training objectives (HRED, language modeling), and alternative dimensionality reduction methods; isolate contribution of each component to overall performance. (6) Clarify practical utility: specify what correlation threshold is acceptable for deployment; discuss when ADEM is suitable vs. when human evaluation is necessary; provide computational efficiency metrics (runtime, memory) in main text rather than supplemental material. (7) Acknowledge that appropriateness criterion is narrow and may not capture full dialogue quality; discuss implications for real-world deployment and propose multi-dimensional evaluation framework. Your transparent acknowledgment of limitations is valuable; consider integrating proposed solutions into the current work rather than deferring to future work.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper reformulates dialogue evaluation as a supervised learning problem, proposing ADEM (Automatic Dialogue Evaluation Model) to predict human appropriateness judgements. The work combines hierarchical RNN encoders with VHRED pre-training and dot-product scoring, demonstrating substantial improvements over word-overlap metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR) at both utterance-level (r=0.436 vs. r<0.15 baselines) and system-level (r=0.954 on 4 models). The contribution is well-motivated, empirically comprehensive, and transparently acknowledges limitations. However, the work is bounded by moderate absolute correlation (81% unexplained variance), weak generalization to certain model types (Dual Encoder r=0.027), limited statistical power for system-level claims (n=4, p=0.046), and domain specificity to Twitter.

Strengths:
- Clear problem motivation: Word-overlap metrics fail for dialogue (Table 2: BLEU-2 r=0.081, ROUGE r=0.114) due to high response diversity; establishes strong baseline for comparison
- Substantial empirical improvement: ADEM achieves 3-5x higher utterance-level correlation than baselines (r=0.436 vs. r<0.15), with statistical significance p<0.001
- Excellent system-level ranking: ADEM achieves r=0.954 system-level correlation, nearly perfect ranking of dialogue models vs. scattered baseline results
- Thoughtful architectural design: Hierarchical RNN encoder is well-motivated for dialogue structure; dot-product scoring is interpretable with only 2 learned matrices
- Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Utterance-level, system-level, generalization (leave-one-out), ablation studies (C-ADEM, R-ADEM), and qualitative error analysis
- Effective semi-supervised pre-training: VHRED pre-training improves performance 52% over tweet2vec (r=0.436 vs. r=0.287), reducing labeled data requirements
- Thoughtful dataset contribution: 4,104 human-annotated responses across 4 diverse sources with reasonable inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.63)
- Transparent acknowledgment of limitations: Authors explicitly identify appropriateness criterion narrowness, generic response bias, conservative prediction bias, and domain specificity

Limitations:
- Moderate absolute correlation (r=0.436) leaves 81% unexplained variance; practical utility for single-response evaluation unclear; no confidence intervals provided to characterize statistical uncertainty or compare to inter-rater reliability ceiling
- System-level evaluation uses only 4 models with marginal statistical significance (p=0.046); small sample size makes correlation unstable; generalization to larger and more diverse model sets unknown
- Generalization to unseen models is partial and unexplained: strong for HRED (r=0.148) and TF-IDF (r=0.196), but fails completely for Dual Encoder (r=0.027, p=0.736 not significant); authors do not investigate why Dual Encoder fails or whether this indicates fundamental architectural limitation
- Domain specificity not validated: trained and evaluated exclusively on Twitter dialogue; generalization to other dialogue domains (Reddit, customer service, task-oriented) not tested; VHRED pre-training requires large unlabeled corpus, limiting transferability
- Appropriateness criterion is narrow and insufficient: does not capture engagement, informativeness, coherence, diversity, or other dialogue qualities; authors acknowledge in Discussion that appropriateness 'does not fully capture the desired end-goal of chatbot systems'; generic response bias identified but not addressed
- Conservative prediction bias due to squared error loss: ADEM tends to predict scores closer to mean (Table 5, third context); alternative loss functions (ranking losses, quantile regression) not explored; magnitude of bias not quantified
- Incomplete ablation studies: no comparison to alternative architectures (Transformer, CNN, attention mechanisms), alternative pre-training objectives (HRED, language modeling), or alternative dimensionality reduction methods; which design choices drive performance unclear
- Computational efficiency claims not quantified: authors claim 'fast evaluation' but provide no runtime comparisons in main text; efficiency details relegated to supplemental material without specific numbers

Open Questions:
- Why does ADEM fail to generalize to Dual Encoder responses (r=0.027, p=0.736 not significant) while generalizing to HRED (r=0.148) and TF-IDF (r=0.196)? Is this a model-specific limitation, architectural mismatch, or fundamental constraint?
- Is r=0.436 utterance-level correlation sufficient for practical deployment in dialogue system development? What is the acceptable threshold for single-response evaluation? How does ADEM performance compare to inter-rater reliability ceiling effect (κ=0.63)?
- How does ADEM generalize to dialogue domains beyond Twitter (Reddit, customer service, task-oriented dialogue)? Does VHRED pre-training transfer to domains without large unlabeled corpora? What is the cost of domain-specific pre-training?
- What is the magnitude of generic response bias in ADEM predictions? How much do ADEM scores correlate with response length and genericity? Can proposed mitigation strategies (censoring, adversarial evaluation) effectively address this bias?
- How much does conservative prediction bias (due to squared error loss) impact practical utility? Would alternative loss functions (ranking losses, quantile regression, focal loss) improve performance?
- Which design choices drive ADEM performance? How much does VHRED pre-training contribute vs. hierarchical RNN architecture? Would alternative pre-training objectives (HRED, language modeling) achieve similar results?
- Can ADEM be extended to handle multiple reference responses? How does single-reference assumption affect evaluation of diverse but appropriate responses?
- What is the computational cost of ADEM inference vs. baselines (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, tweet2vec)? Is the model truly 'fast' as claimed?

Transparency:
Authors transparently acknowledge multiple limitations (appropriateness criterion narrowness, generic response bias, conservative prediction bias, domain specificity) and propose concrete future directions. However, the paper defers critical issues to future work rather than addressing them in the current contribution. Computational efficiency claims are not quantified in main text. Dual Encoder generalization failure is reported but not investigated. Inter-rater reliability ceiling effect is not quantified. The paper would benefit from: (1) confidence intervals for all correlation estimates, (2) investigation of Dual Encoder failure, (3) quantification of identified biases, (4) preliminary domain transfer validation, (5) comprehensive ablation studies, (6) computational efficiency metrics in main text.

top_documents.title: Document 3
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.
